query: Sealed With Wax {a} presses a folded note into your hand, sealed with candle wax and, by the look of it, a great deal of worry. "For {b}. Don't read it. Don't let {b.them} open it in front of anyone. Don't say it's from me." You point out that {b} will know who it's from. {a} looks stricken. Deliver it as asked You find {b} alone in the library and hand it over. {b} reads it twice, goes pink to the ears, and asks you, with great dignity, to tell {a} "yes. Probably. Thursday." {b} reads it in the library and goes quiet. "Tell {a} it's very kind," {b.they} say{b.s}, which is the worst thing anyone can say. You carry it back as gently as you can. Help {a} write it better You sit up with {a} over four drafts, crossing out the poetry. What's left is three plain lines, the best thing {a} has ever written, and {b} answers them the same evening. You find out how it went at breakfast, from the way they arrive together. By the fourth draft it's a sonnet, and a bad one, and {a} has gone off the whole idea. "I'll just tell {b.them}. One day." The note stays in {their} pocket for the rest of the term. You can see the corner of it.

results.excerpt:
A Secret Admirer
Folded notes keep appearing in your library books. Unsigned. They're funny, and a little nervous, and they know things about you that only someone paying attention would know. The handwriting looks familiar.
Leave a note back
You write back. The notes get longer.

The Wrong Letter
